posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

Death isn't a single switch that shuts down your entire body at once. When your heart stops beating and your brain goes silent, trillions of cells inside you are still alive, desperately trying to keep themselves running. Death isn't a single moment, but a slow and surprisingly complex process that can last for weeks.

What actually happens when you die? What makes death so mysterious, and which cells are the last survivors within your body? Watch our full video to find out!

recentPosts.caption:
The daring food choices you can make in Bangkok… and that's part of the adventure. 😂⁠
From unfamiliar ingredients to unexpected street food combinations, Thailand has a way of taking your taste buds out of their comfort zone. ⁠
⁠
Sometimes the best travel stories start with a bite you weren't quite sure about!⁠
Would you be brave enough to try it? 👀⁠
🎥: @rootedinsummer

This phenomenon is called Chicagohenge, and it happens when the setting sun lines up perfectly with the city’s streets, something that only happens around the spring and fall equinoxes. ⁠
⁠
The photographer, @theurban.traveller captured these magical shots as the sunset glowed through the windows and the passengers turned into silhouettes. 😍⁠
⁠
P.S. Did you notice the heart between the two silhouettes?

Not every dance ends on the dance floor… some end on broken glass!⁠
 A fascinating variation of the traditional Minangkabau Plate Dance from West Sumatra. ⁠
What starts with rhythmic movements and plates in the dancers' hands builds up to an unbelievable finale, as performers dance barefoot over sharp pieces of broken glass.⁠
⁠
Rooted in Minangkabau heritage, this performance is a striking expression of tradition, skill and cultural identity.⁠
⁠
One of those experiences that makes you realise ju

@kamranonbike captured these striking portraits of people in Ghana and Sierra Leone, each carrying their goods on their heads.⁠
⁠
Across West Africa, people carry everything this way, from eggs and fruit to water, clothes, and cooking pots, often walking long distances all day. ⁠
⁠
It looks effortless, but it’s a skill many learn in childhood. Despite the weight, everyone in it stands tall and proud 🤍⁠
⁠
Which portrait stands out to you the most?

A flower fit for a Himalayan legend. 🤍🌸⁠
Meet Brahma Kamal, famously known as the King of Himalayan Flowers. ⁠
Found in the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas, this rare and striking bloom holds deep cultural and spiritual significance, making it much more than just a beautiful sight.⁠
⁠
Nature really has a way of creating something extraordinary.⁠
🎥: @kailsati18

Saudi Arabia is getting its first luxury sleeper train, and it’s designed to make the desert part of the journey.⁠
⁠
Called Dream of the Desert, the train will set off from Riyadh, starting in October 2027, taking guests across the kingdom to the mountains of Hail, the oases of Al Qassim and the historic sites of Al Jouf. ⁠
⁠
On board, they’ll stay in private suite cabins designed by Lebanese architect Aline Asmar d’Amman and her studio, Culture in Architecture.⁠
⁠
Tag someone you’d take on this

@jorgemchagas captured Lisbon on a foggy day, when the city’s streets and its famous bridge seemed to disappear into the mist.⁠
⁠
On days like this, the whole city feels quiet, dreamy, and mysterious. 😍⁠
⁠
Which photo is your favorite?

@amsubbu captured this tender moment as a mother polar bear touched noses with her cub in the fog.⁠
⁠
It was a dream encounter for him. Polar bears depend on sea ice to hunt seals. As the Arctic warms, the ice forms later and melts earlier, leaving bears to spend longer on land, waiting and fasting until it returns⁠.⁠
⁠
Share this with someone to make their day better!

These tiny harvest mice at the British Wildlife Centre look right at home climbing autumn gourds.⁠
⁠
As Britain’s smallest rodent, a harvest mouse weighs about the same as a British 2p coin. That light build lets them climb and balance on thin stems, using their tails like an extra hand. ⁠
⁠
They can even sense vibrations through their feet, warning them when larger animals are nearby.⁠
⁠
The centre also breeds harvest mice and releases them into its own nature reserve to help boost local popula

@letsgoto_pl captured the Earth Pyramids of Longomoso in South Tyrol, Italy, tall pillars of earth that look almost unreal.⁠
⁠
They formed after glaciers left behind a mix of soil and rocks. Rain slowly washed away the softer earth, but the big stones on top protected the ground below, leaving these towering columns behind. Once a stone falls, the pillar beneath it begins to wear away, too.⁠
⁠
Would you hike to see these up close?

A galaxy hidden beneath the ocean. 🌌🌊⁠
This deep-sea view looks almost otherworldly, with glowing blue lights and tiny points of bioluminescence scattered through the darkness. ⁠
⁠
The deeper you go, the more it feels like you're looking into space rather than the ocean.⁠
Turns out, some of the most unreal sights aren't above us, but way below. ✨⁠
🎥: @pelagicblonde

A cloud shaped like a giant bird spread its wings over Mount Fuji, and the photographer was there to capture it. 😍⁠
⁠
It’s a lenticular cloud, a smooth, lens-shaped cloud that forms when strong winds flow up and over a mountain. Mount Fuji is famous for them, and they can take on all kinds of surprising shapes.⁠
⁠
By: @kenken710

In Pakistan, kitschy and bombastic images are often sold as souvenirs at festivals and large social gatherings. After discovering them in 2021, photographer and National Geographic Explorer Matthieu Paley spent five years collecting these unique prints from different events and pilgrimages. Featuring fantastical depictions of actresses, soldiers, and fancy estates, the images are not about precision—they're about spectacle.

See more of these prints at the link in bio.

The 1,847 islands of Raja Ampat, Indonesia, are home to more than 1,600 known species of fish, including manta rays, leopard sharks, and brown coral blennies. Thanks to the work of marine scientist Mark Erdmann, Indonesia banned commercial fishing and resource extraction across the islands around 20 years ago, designating much of the archipelago as a network of marine protected areas. Discover more about our one ocean at the link in bio. 

Rolex and The National Geographic Society are partnering on select science-based expeditions to explore, study, and document change in the planet’s unique regions. #PerpetualPlanet.

Road collisions in Brazil have killed hundreds of giant anteaters and left many pups orphaned and in need of rehabilitation. At rehab centers, the young animals receive medical care as they regain their strength and are prepared for their possible reintroduction to the wild. National Geographic Explorer @fernando.faciole spent three years documenting these elusive mammals and the efforts underway to protect them.

Learn more about the threats giant anteaters face in Brazil at the link in bio.

The mosque’s elegant minarets and white marbled domes decorate the horizon, and I loved shooting here at dawn when the cool light of the evening sky mixes with the warm light of the sun.

An ecosystem needs more than just its predators to survive, but wolves help keep much of it in balance. By influencing prey populations and where other animals feed, they can affect everything from vegetation growth to biodiversity. After following a pack in Canada for eight years for his new series #WolvesUpClose, National Geographic Explorer @bertiegregory shares what he observed about their lives in the wild.

Discover more at the link in bio.

Photographer and National Geographic Explorer Morgan Heim (@moheim) captured conservationist Matt Trevelyan walking through the Nidderdale valley in northern England, dressed in a handcrafted Eurasian curlew costume. Trevelyan wears the costume to raise awareness about the near-threatened bird's vanishing habitat in the English moors. He's even worn it on a 53-mile hike and to London's Parliament.
